name: Liam Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at Redbank, the big open-pit copper mine outside Kellerton. It's a 220-tonne truck, and I do twelve-hour shifts, four days on and four off, running ore from the shovel to the crusher and waste to the dump. I've been there two years and I'm still one of the slow ones, still getting yelled at over the radio for bad spotting under the shovel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cab at five in the morning when the pit's lit up and it's just me and the radio. I like the pay, and I like the crew in the crib room, especially Gaz, who's been driving thirty years. What wears me out is nights, the dust, and the feeling that the company counts every minute I sit in the queue. My partner Nadia's a nurse on shifts too, so some weeks we only see each other asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, that it's a lot of noise from people who've never been down a haul road. At smoko I'd tell the boys the company still needs bums in seats. Online I don't really post, but I'd share something from the union saying we told you so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even with AI being hype, the driverless trucks aren't hype. Mintor (another mining company) already runs them at its pit two hours north, and that has nothing to do with chatbots. So I'd still be looking over my shoulder, just not as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to get my spotting good enough to move onto the shovel. I'd keep putting the four hundred a fortnight into savings like Nadia and I agreed. And I'd keep going to union meetings, because that's where you hear things first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of a knot still there. It's like a storm that goes around you, but you can still see it over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the driverless trucks aren't hype. What would you say to Gaz about that over lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gaz would tell me I'm worrying like an old woman. Then I'd point out that my mate Gaz retires in four years and I've got forty years left. Gaz has already won and I'm still at the start of the race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your savings in this picture? Do they grow, or does something eat them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent in Kellerton's gone up twice since the mine expanded, so a lot of it gets eaten. We've got about four months put away. Without a crisis we'd maybe get to six and think about a deposit on a house.

say: I'd call AI **mostly noise** from people who've never driven a haul road.
I'd tell the crew the company still needs **drivers in seats**.
think: Driverless trucks at **Mintor's pit** are real, whatever happens with chatbots.
My job is **safe for now**, but I still watch it closely.
do: Keep putting **$400 a fortnight** into savings with Nadia.
Practise spotting to move up to the **shovel** within a year.
Keep going to **union meetings** to hear news early.
feel: **Relief** that the storm misses, with a **knot** still there about the trucks.
S0.quote: My mate Gaz retires in four years and I've got forty years left.
fieldNote: Liam separates **AI hype** from mine robots and still worries about trucks even in the calm picture.
His **union** is where he gets his information, not the internet.
Rising **rent** in a boom town eats the savings he would otherwise build.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck and practise spotting under the shovel
Put $400 a fortnight into the joint savings account
Go to every union meeting at the Kellerton hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table before the company buys anything. At work I'd be telling people to sign up, the young ones especially. Online I'd share stuff about other mines that went driverless and what the workers got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office people go first in this one, the dispatchers and the planners. But once the company's saved money there, it'll want the trucks next, and Redbank's pit is perfect for driverless trucks. When the mine cuts the driver roster, a junior like me is first on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the union's automation committee if they have one, or push them to start one. I'd ask the superintendent straight out what the truck plan is for the next three years. And I'd stop eating out and save harder, maybe get the cushion to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, to be honest. I don't like change and I'm not good with screens, so being told to change how I work scares me more than I'd say at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good with screens. If the company offered you a job in the control room running driverless trucks, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say yes, but I'd probably be bad at it. My mate Ash (another driver) did a computer course for the dispatch job and failed twice. I'd rather be on the dozer or doing something with my hands that a truck can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on days off, and the new ute I've been looking at. Nadia wants a holiday next winter and I'd ask her to wait a year.

say: I'd say the **union** needs to be at the table before any new tech is bought.
I'd push the **young drivers** to sign up now.
think: Office jobs like **dispatch** go first, then the company comes for the trucks.
As a **junior driver**, I'd be first off the roster.
do: Join or start a **union automation committee** in the first months.
Ask the **superintendent** directly about the truck plan for three years.
Cut takeaway and the **new ute** to reach six months saved.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, more scared of changing how he works than he'd admit.
S1.quote: When the mine cuts the driver roster, a junior like me is first on the list.
fieldNote: He sees **office cuts** as a warning sign for drivers, not as separate.
He doubts he could pass a **control room** course and would rather stay hands-on.
Postponing **Nadia's holiday** is the first real cost he names.

steps.text: Push the union to start an automation committee at Redbank
Skip the new ute and takeaway to reach six months saved
Ask the superintendent what the driverless truck plan is

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to stop this or pay for it, full stop. At work I'd be loud about it, maybe too loud. Online I'd finally post, probably something angry about the owners getting rich off machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 the planners and dispatch are gone, and by 2031 the trucks drive themselves. That gives me three years in the cab and then nothing. I've got secondary school and a truck ticket, and the truck ticket won't be worth anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd save every dollar I can, maybe stop paying into the car and sell it. I'd go to every union rally and back any party promising a wage guarantee for miners. If Redbank started cutting drivers, I'd try for a fitter's apprenticeship, though I'd be old for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor goes out under the truck. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be old for an apprenticeship. Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Gaz, then the training lady at the site office. But those robots are coming for fitters too, three years after, so I don't know what the point is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Nadia's job fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nadia's job is the one I'm not worried about. Robots aren't changing bedpans by 2031. If it comes to it, Nadia carries us for a while, and I hate that, but I'd have to swallow it.

say: I'd demand the **government** stops it or pays for it.
I'd finally post online, angry at **owners** getting rich off machines.
think: **Dispatch and planning** go by 2028, and the trucks by **2031**.
My **truck ticket** will be worth nothing, and I've only got secondary school.
do: Sell the car and **save every dollar** over the next two years.
Join every **union rally** and vote for a miners' wage guarantee.
Ask about a **fitter's apprenticeship** if Redbank starts cutting drivers.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor dropping out from under the truck.
S2.quote: My partner Nadia's job is the one I'm not worried about. Robots aren't changing bedpans by 2031.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** gives him a little time but no plan he believes in.
He leans on **Nadia's** nursing income and hates that he has to.
His anger points at **owners and government**, not at the technology itself.

steps.text: Sell the car and save every spare dollar for two years
Join union rallies for a guaranteed wage for laid-off miners
Vote for the party promising support for miners who lose work
Rely on Nadia's nursing pay if the driving job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before but less shouting. I'd say we have five years, so the union and the company should sit down now and agree on what happens to the drivers. I'd tell friends this isn't the end of the world yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still the same end. The trucks go around 2034, I'd be 35, and that's too young to stop and too old to start over easily. Five years just means I worry longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to bargain for a retraining fund in the next agreement, which comes up in 2028. I'd keep driving and save, and maybe go back to the training lady about the fitter's course while I'm still under 30. I'd tell Nadia we should hold off buying a house until we know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Not panic, but like carrying a full crib bag up the ramp every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said twice you'd ask about the fitter's course. What stops you actually signing up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, I suppose. I left school and swore I'd never sit an exam again. And I'd be on apprentice pay for four years, which is half what I earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would holding off on a house mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another five years renting off Mr Pillay (their landlord), probably. Nadia wants kids at some point, and a house first. That's the bit that gets me. A driverless truck could decide when my partner Nadia and I start a family.

say: I'd say the **union and company** should agree now on what happens to drivers.
I'd tell friends it's **not the end** yet.
think: The end point is the same, with trucks gone around **2034** when I'm 35.
**Five years** just means I worry for longer.
do: Push for a **retraining fund** in the 2028 agreement.
Hold off on **buying a house** with Nadia until things are clear.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying a full crib bag up the ramp every day.
S3.quote: A driverless truck could decide when my partner Nadia and I start a family.
fieldNote: The extra years don't lift him because he can't picture **starting over** at 35.
**Fear of exams** and apprentice pay keep him from the fitter's course.
The **house and kids** plan is where the threat feels most personal.

steps.text: Push the union for a retraining fund in the 2028 agreement
Delay buying a house with Nadia until the truck plan is clear
Keep driving the haul truck and wait for the company's plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, if the government makes the companies pay. At work I'd say it's not our problem yet. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years and three more for the robots is thirteen years of driving. I'd be 40. That's a real stretch of work, and I might have the shovel or a dozer ticket by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and try to get onto the shovel in the next two years. I'd keep saving and probably buy a house with Nadia, because a mortgage would be fine if I've got ten-plus years of pay ahead. I'd stay in the union and keep pushing for a retraining plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. A bit anxious still, because at 40 I'd have a mortgage and maybe kids and no trade. But it feels like a problem for future me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a problem for future me. What would future you wish you'd done now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably done the fitter's course at 27 instead of 37. I know that, I just don't like hearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine paid for the fitter's course and kept my wage, I'd do it tomorrow. If I'm paying, I'll keep driving and hope.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do it properly if companies pay.
At work I'd call it **not our problem** yet.
think: That's about **thirteen years** of driving, until I'm around 40.
At 40 I'd have a **mortgage** and maybe kids, but no trade.
do: Move up to the **shovel** within two years.
Buy a **house** with Nadia using the savings as a deposit.
Keep pushing the union for a **retraining plan**.
feel: **Better**, with a low hum of worry left for the future.
S4.quote: If the mine paid for the fitter's course and kept my wage, I'd do it tomorrow.
fieldNote: The longer warning moves him from **dread** to putting things off.
He knows he should **retrain now** and admits he won't unless it's paid.
**Company-funded** training is the one thing that would change what he does.

steps.text: Train to operate the shovel within two years
Use the savings as a house deposit with Nadia
Keep pressing the union for company-paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one that scares me, because three years in the cab isn't enough to become something else. What would help is a deal where Redbank pays for my apprenticeship and keeps my wage while I do it. A government wage guarantee for miners would help too, so nobody's left in Kellerton with no job and a truck ticket.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If Redbank goes driverless, it's not just us. The pub, the footy club and the mechanic all live off our wages, and Kellerton could just empty out. My truck ticket is the only thing I've got, and a robot that drives itself makes my truck ticket worthless.

headlineQuote: My truck ticket is the only thing I've got, and a robot that drives itself makes my truck ticket worthless.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old haul truck driver** at Redbank, a large open-pit copper mine, two years in and still learning.
He lives with **Nadia**, a nurse, rents in Kellerton and has about **four months** saved.
A strong **union** man who avoids screens and new tech, he blames owners and government rather than machines.
His mood darkens with each faster **AGI** picture, because driverless trucks would take his only skill.
He knows he should **retrain** as a fitter now, but won't unless the company pays.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years in the cab isn't enough time to become something else.
whatWouldHelp: A **company-paid apprenticeship** that keeps his wage while he trains.
A government **wage guarantee** for miners so Kellerton doesn't empty out.
